extracted.intended_audience: political communication and media effects researchers; social scientists studying media use and partisan behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical standards for measuring selective exposure in political contexts using survey and panel data, including variable construction, measurement choices, controls, and analytic tests for moderation and causal direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of selective exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective exposure — the selection of information matching their beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames selective exposure as people seeking out likeminded views and argues certain topics (such as politics) are more likely to inspire selective exposure. Research should investigate habitual media exposure patterns rather than single exposure decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media types as separate dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media types (newspapers, political talk radio, cable news, and Internet) are treated as distinct domains for selective exposure analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study investigates whether these media types are more or less likely to inspire selective exposure and reports patterns across media types; analytic models are run separately by media type and over time for cable news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a nationally representative panel dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the 2004 National Annenberg Election Survey (NAES) for cross-sectional and over-time/panel analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NAES provides content-based exposure measures and allows over-time analyses to assess whether political beliefs motivate media use patterns and how audiences change during a campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based media exposure measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Media dependent variables measured content-based exposure (as opposed to frequency of exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content-based exposure may be easier for respondents to accurately recall and is preferred here; it increases confidence in linking political predispositions to media exposure even if self-reports are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended outlet/program naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents were asked open-ended questions about their media exposure, requiring recall of the name of the media program or outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended naming helps validate content-based exposure measures because respondents must recall specific outlets/programs rather than selecting from a provided list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining partisanship and ideology into a single political predisposition measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Partisanship and ideology measures were combined to create a single measure of political predispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: work shows partisanship and ideology have become increasingly consistent over time. Analyses were also run with partisanship and ideology entered separately or as a categorical variable; results are reported as robust to these specifications (with noted exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variables incorporated throughout analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls (demographics and other variables listed in the appendix) are incorporated throughout the analysis to help take into account differences between the population and the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls include education, income, race/ethnicity, gender, age, media use measures, political discussion, political interest, general political knowledge, and strength of ideology/partisanship; see appendix for coding and descriptive statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media use frequency coding (0–7 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media use was measured by asking how many days in the past week (0–7) respondents used each media type (e.g., watched national network news, watched 24h cable news, read a newspaper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interval-style variables are recoded and summarized (means and SDs reported) and used as media use measures in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to campaign stories scale (0–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media attention measured with response options: no attention at all (0), not too much, some, and a great deal of attention (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate attention measures reported for national network/cable TV, local TV, and newspapers; means and SDs provided and used to capture depth of attention beyond frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet access and political internet use coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet access coded yes/no (76.2% have access); used the Internet for political information measured (mean reported); those without Internet access were coded as 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two questions (access information online; read information online) were combined into one variable after checking distributions and means; coding decisions and handling of non-users are explicitly documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining similar survey items when distributions align
rubrics_metrics.description: Two questions about online political information (how many days did you access information online? and how many days did you read information online?) were combined into one variable because they had similar distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means and SDs for the two items are reported and the combined variable is used throughout analysis; documents rationale for combining near-duplicative items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skip and non-consumer coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Only respondents indicating that they consumed each of the various types of media were asked follow-up questions about that medium; those indicating they did not consume each media type were coded as 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This handling avoids asking non-users about content and ensures non-consumption is treated explicitly rather than missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: General political knowledge battery and coding
rubrics_metrics.description: General political knowledge battery of 5 items; responses collapsed into a dichotomous measure where scores of A and B were coded as 1 and C, D, and F coded as 0 (α = 0.64).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items covered Cheney’s job, constitutional adjudication, veto override rules, House majority party, and interviewer’s assessment of knowledgeability; don't know and refused responses were coded as incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of ideology/partisanship scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength of ideology/partisanship measured on a 0–4 scale, with higher values indicating stronger leanings (M = 1.83, SD = 1.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength is used as a covariate and to differentiate intensity of attachments; categorical and separate ideology/partisanship specifications are also tested for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing demographic moderation via interaction terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses incorporate interactions between ideology/partisanship and age and between ideology/partisanship and gender to evaluate whether demographics moderate selective exposure patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results reported as inconsistent; specific marginal/significant interactions are described (e.g., younger liberal Democrats more likely to listen to liberal radio), and three-way interactions with time were also tested for over-time moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel analyses for causal direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel analyses conducted to examine reverse causal direction — whether partisan media use contributes to ideology/partisanship (media → political identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: in some instances listening to conservative talk radio and watching FOX related to being a stronger conservative Republican, and watching CNN/MSNBC and accessing liberal websites related to being a stronger liberal Democrat. Interpretations include learning political labels vs media changing/intensifying identities; caution about interpretation during heated campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks across variable specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses repeated with partisanship and ideology entered separately, and with a categorical ideology/partisanship variable to check robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results are generally unchanged across specifications, with noted exceptions (e.g., liberal websites where liberal Democrats were no more likely than those without attachments to access them). Exceptions and p-values are reported where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of measurement debate and confidence-boosting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that there is some debate about the accuracy of survey-based media exposure measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note two components that may boost confidence in their measures: (1) content-based exposure is easier to recall than frequency; (2) open-ended naming of programs/outlets. They also note that even if measures are imperfect, reported associations still imply recognition/reporting of congenial outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of variable availability and subset analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some survey questions were present only for parts of the period; when such variables are employed the analysis covers only a subset of dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors document item removal dates (e.g., one item removed Oct 8–10, 2004) and random subsampling for certain batteries (e.g., general political knowledge asked of a random two-thirds at specific periods); analyses transparently account for these design features.
